summary: Describes evaluation test cases for congestion control of interactive real-time media over wireless networks, where capacity and delay can change quickly. It supports testing RTP-based congestion control for a good user experience. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8869 extends the congestion control test plan to wireless. It explains what makes a cellular link different from a wired one, sets out two cellular scenarios and several Wi-Fi ones with their parameters, and says what a good result looks like in each. The recommended way to run them is in a network simulator, because a real cellular network cannot be made repeatable.

questions: how to test rtp congestion control over wireless
what test cases exist for wireless media
what are cellular network test cases for rtp
how do you evaluate algorithms on wi-fi networks
subtitle: Test scenarios for judging a congestion control algorithm over cellular and Wi-Fi access links.

tldr.problem: The lab test cases in RFC 8867 assume a wired path, and a wireless access link behaves quite differently: capacity can change within milliseconds, queues are per user rather than per link, and handovers interrupt traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines test cases for cellular networks, covering varying network load and bad radio coverage, and test cases for Wi-Fi, covering a bottleneck in the wired segment and a bottleneck in the wireless segment, each with a full parameter set and a stated expected behaviour.
tldr.outcome: Because deterministic testing on an operational cellular network is not possible, the RFC recommends running the cellular cases on a simulator, and it says the same of the Wi-Fi cases, while still encouraging testbed checks with real equipment where feasible.

today: RFC 8869 is an Informational document from January 2021 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It extends the test plan of RFC 8867 to cellular and Wi-Fi access links, and its cellular and Wi-Fi parameter sets remain the reference for anyone evaluating a congestion control proposal over a wireless network.

sections.title: Why Wireless Needs Its Own Test Cases
sections.content:
Wireless networks, both cellular and Wi-Fi, are an integral and increasingly significant part of the Internet, and typical application scenarios for interactive multimedia over wireless include video calls from a bus or train and live streaming at home. The characteristics and technical challenges of supporting multimedia over wireless are very different from those of providing the same service over a wired network. The basic test cases in RFC 8867 cover many common effects of network impairments, but they still have to be tested over the characteristics and dynamics unique to a given wireless environment.

In a cellular network, for example, the base station maintains individual queues per radio bearer per user, which leads to a different nature of interaction between the traffic flows of different users. This contrasts with a wired network setting, where traffic flows from all users share the same queue at the bottleneck. User mobility patterns in a cellular network also differ from those in a Wi-Fi network. RFC 8868 recognizes the importance of testing over wireless access networks but describes no specific test cases; this document describes test cases targeting cellular and Wi-Fi networks specifically.

A cellular environment is more complicated than its wireline counterpart because it provides service in the context of variable available bandwidth, location dependencies and user mobilities at different speeds. A user may reach the cell edge, which can lead to a significant number of retransmissions to deliver data to and from the base station. Those radio links often act as a bottleneck for the rest of the network, leading to excessive delays or packet drops. An efficient retransmission or link adaptation mechanism can reduce the packet loss probability, but some loss and delay variation remain. With increased cell load or a handover to a congested cell, congestion in the transport network becomes even worse.
sections.plainLanguage: A wireless link does not behave like a wired one. In a cell, each user has their own queue instead of sharing one, the amount each user may send is set by the network, and the usable capacity changes with distance, speed and interference, sometimes within milliseconds. A test that only uses a wired path would miss all of that.

sections.title: The Cellular Test Cases
sections.content:
Several characteristics distinguish a cellular network from other wireless access networks such as Wi-Fi. The bottleneck is often a shared link with relatively few users, and the cost per bit over that shared link varies over time and differs between users, with leftover resources that can be consumed by other greedy users. Queues are always per radio bearer, so each user can have many such queues. Users can experience both inter- and intra-Radio Access Technology handovers. A handover between cells or a change of serving cell might cause user plane interruptions, leading to bursts of packet loss, delay and jitter; the exact behaviour depends on the type of radio bearer, and typically the default best-effort bearers do not generate packet loss, instead queueing packets and transmitting them once the handover is complete. The network part decides how much the user can transmit. The cellular network has variable link capacity per user, which can vary as fast as a period of milliseconds, depends on many factors such as distance, speed, interference and different flows, and uses complex and smart link adaptation that makes the link behaviour ever more dynamic; the scheduling priority depends on the estimated throughput. Both Quality of Service and non-QoS radio bearers can be used.

So a real-time application over a cellular network has to cope with a shared bottleneck link and variable link capacity, events like handover, loss that has nothing to do with congestion, and abrupt changes in bandwidth both short term and long term. The key factors in defining the test cases are shared and varying link capacity, mobility, and handover, but these are highly correlated in a cellular network, so instead of separate test cases for individual events the document divides them into two categories. The goal is to evaluate performance over the radio interface, so the radio interface is assumed to be the bottleneck link between the communicating peers and the core network is assumed to add no extra congestion along the path. The combination of cellular and Wi-Fi users is therefore out of scope, since the shared bottleneck there is likely at the wired backhaul link. The cases assume a typical real-time telephony scenario in which one session consists of one voice stream and one video stream.

Although it is possible to test over operational cellular networks, and such tests are available, they cannot in general be carried out deterministically to ensure repeatability: the networks are controlled by operators and carry competing traffic in the same cells. In practice it is only in underground mines that near-deterministic testing is possible, and even there it is not guaranteed, since workers carry their own phones, and the mining setting may not reflect typical urban usage. The RFC therefore recommends a cellular network simulator for these test cases, for example the LTE simulator in ns-3.

The first cellular test case, varying network load, evaluates performance under changing load, created by adding and removing users during the simulation. Each user in the media session is an endpoint following RTP-based congestion control, and user arrivals follow a Poisson distribution proportional to the length of the call, to keep the number of users per cell fairly constant during the evaluation period. There should be enough time at the beginning to warm up the network, so that the evaluation is not run in an empty network with empty buffers and low interference; that initialization period is excluded, and the evaluation period typically starts 30 seconds after test initialization. The test also includes user mobility and competing traffic, of both the same types of flows with the same adaptation algorithms and different types with different services and congestion control schemes.

The second cellular test case, bad radio coverage, evaluates performance when users visit part of the network with poor coverage, created by using a larger cell radius than in the previous case. The expected behaviour in both cellular cases is the same: the investigated algorithms should give maximum possible network utilization, stability in terms of rate variations, the lowest possible end-to-end frame latency and network latency, and the lowest Packet Loss Rate at different cell load levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Two cellular cases are defined. The first changes the number of users in the cell during the run, so the load goes up and down. The second gives the cell a much larger radius, so users sit in worse coverage. In both, the algorithm should keep the network busy without the rate jumping around, keep delay and loss as low as possible, and do so at every load level.

sections.title: The Cellular Simulation Setup
sections.content:
Each mobile user is connected to a fixed user. The connection consists of a cellular radio access, an Evolved Packet Core and an Internet connection, with the mobile user reaching the core over the radio access technology and the fixed user reaching the Internet over a wired connection with sufficiently high bandwidth, for instance 10 Gbps, so that the system bottleneck sits on the cellular radio interface. That wired connection adds no impairments to the test, only 10 ms of one-way propagation delay. The path from the fixed user to the mobile users is the downlink, and the path from the mobile users to the fixed user is the uplink; since only one of the two is assumed to be congested, the RFC recommends running the uplink and downlink simulations separately.

Values in brackets follow the same notion as in RFC 8867, meaning that a separate test is run for each value. The radio environment uses the 3GPP case 1 deployment and propagation model, a Multiple-Input and Multiple-Output antenna with a 2D or 3D pattern, mobility of either 3 km/h or 30 km/h, a transmission bandwidth of 10 MHz, a multi-cell deployment of 3 cells per base station times 7 base stations, giving 21 cells, a cell radius of 166.666 meters, a proportional fair scheduler with no priority, a default bearer for all traffic, and Active Queue Management either on or off. The end-to-end round trip time is either 40 ms or 150 ms, and users arrive following a Poisson arrival model.

User intensity is given as a list of values to sweep. The downlink simulation uses the set from 0.7 to 10.5 and the uplink simulation the set from 0.7 to 7.0, in steps of 0.7. The simulation runs 91 s and the evaluation period is 30 s to 60 s.

Media traffic is one video source per user and one audio source per user, each running for 30 s, in either the uplink or the downlink direction. The video source is the one defined in section 4.3 of RFC 8867. The audio source uses a constant bit rate codec at 20 Kbps with adaptation off. The other traffic models are web browsing or FTP traffic following the default TCP congestion control, with a maximum of 4 Mbps per cell in the downlink simulation and 2 Mbps per cell in the uplink simulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The cellular lab is a 21-cell network with a 10 MHz radio band and users moving at 3 or 30 km/h. The run lasts 91 seconds, but only the half-minute from 30 to 60 seconds is scored, so that the network has settled down first. The number of users per cell is swept through a list of values, and the test is run separately for the uplink and the downlink.

sections.title: The Wi-Fi Test Cases
sections.content:
Wi-Fi access links are so common that candidate RTP-based congestion control solutions have to be evaluated over test cases that include them. The RFC lists the characteristics that differ from the wired case. The wireless radio channel is subject to interference from nearby transmitters, multipath fading and shadowing, which lead to fluctuations in link throughput and sometimes an error-prone communication environment. Available bandwidth is not only shared over the air between concurrent users but also between uplink and downlink traffic, because the wireless transmission medium is half-duplex. Packet transmissions over Wi-Fi are susceptible to contention and collisions over the air, so traffic load beyond a certain utilization level introduces frequent collisions and significant network overhead, along with packet drops from buffer overflow at the transmitters, leading to excessive delay, retransmissions, packet losses and lower effective bandwidth. The collision-induced delay and loss patterns are qualitatively different from those caused by congestion on a wired connection.

The IEEE 802.11 standard supports multi-rate transmission by dynamically choosing the modulation and coding scheme for the received signal strength, and a different choice gives a different physical-layer link rate and so a different application-layer throughput. The presence of legacy devices, such as ones operating only on 802.11b at a much lower link rate, can significantly slow down the rest of a modern Wi-Fi network, because it takes much longer to transmit the same packet over a slower link and so consumes a substantial portion of air time. A handover from one access point to another may lead to excessive packet delays and losses. IEEE 802.11e introduced the Enhanced Distributed Channel Access mechanism, which lets different traffic categories contend for channel access with different random back-off parameters and is a mandatory requirement for Wi-Fi Multimedia certification; it allows real-time traffic such as voice and video to be prioritised over non-urgent transfers.

Unless otherwise mentioned, the test cases choose their physical and MAC layer parameters from the IEEE 802.11n standard. Statistics from enterprise Wi-Fi networks show the two dominant physical modes are 802.11n and 802.11ac, accounting for 41% and 58% of connected devices respectively, so as standards evolve, with the introduction of Wi-Fi 6 based on IEEE 802.11ax, the physical and MAC layer test case specifications need to be updated to match.

Typically a Wi-Fi access network connects to a wired infrastructure, and either the wired or the Wi-Fi segment can be the bottleneck. The two families of test cases cover both scenarios separately, and the same set of performance metrics as in RFC 8867 should be collected for each. The RFC recommends carrying out the test cases using a simulator such as ns-2 or ns-3, and where feasible encourages testbed-based evaluations using real access points and endpoints running up-to-date IEEE 802.11 protocols, so as to verify the viability of the candidate schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Wi-Fi has its own set of troubles: interference and fading make the throughput wobble, the radio is half-duplex so sending and receiving compete, and heavy load causes collisions that look nothing like the congestion seen on a wired link. The test plan therefore covers both a home-style setup where the wired link is the bottleneck and an enterprise-style setup where the wireless link is.

sections.title: The Wi-Fi Scenarios and Expected Behaviour
sections.content:
With the bottleneck in the wired network, the test is meant to mimic video conferencing over Wi-Fi connections from the home, where the home network is not congested and the bottleneck is on the wired access link. The topology holds multiple mobile nodes connected to a common Wi-Fi access point and their corresponding wired clients on fixed nodes, with each connection carrying either an RTP-based media flow or a TCP traffic flow, in the uplink, downlink or both directions. The total number of media flows is N and of TCP flows is M. The setup runs 120 s with a log-distance path loss radio propagation model, IEEE 802.11n physical and MAC layers, an MCS index of 11 giving a raw data rate of 52 Mbps with 16-QAM and a 1/2 coding rate, and a wired path with 1 Mbps capacity, 50 ms one-way propagation delay, 30 ms maximum end-to-end jitter, a drop tail queue of 300 ms and a path loss ratio of 0%. The typical scenarios are a single uplink media flow with N=1 and M=0; a pair of bidirectional media flows with N=2 and M=0; the same pair with an uplink on-off CBR flow over UDP, with M=1, ON from 0 to 60 s and OFF from 60 to 119 s; the same pair with an uplink off-on CBR flow, OFF from 0 to 60 s and ON from 60 to 119 s; and one uplink media flow competing against one long-lived uplink TCP flow, with M=1, running from 0 to 119 s. The expected behaviour is that a single flow detects the path capacity constraint, converges to the bottleneck link capacity and avoids unwanted oscillations; that bidirectional flows converge to the bottleneck capacity of the wired path in both directions despite measurement noise over the Wi-Fi connection, and adapt promptly to the arrival and departure of background traffic; and that a flow competing with a long-lived TCP flow avoids congestion collapse and stabilizes at a fair share of the bottleneck capacity.

With the bottleneck in the Wi-Fi network, the wired segment along the media path is well provisioned, with 100 Mbps capacity, and the same 50 ms delay, 30 ms jitter, drop tail queue of 300 ms and 0% loss, while the wireless access network is the bottleneck. This mimics the enterprise or coffee-house scenario. The scenarios are: multiple media flows sharing the wireless downlink, with N=16 all downlink and M=0, which for an 802.11n network with an MCS index of 11 and a 52 Mbps link rate gives a total application-layer throughput of around 20 Mbps, so 16 flows at up to 1.5 Mbps each are expected to saturate the wireless interface; multiple media flows sharing the wireless uplink, also N=16, where multiple clients transmitting uplink introduce more frequent contentions and potential collisions, so per-flow throughput is expected to be lower than in the downlink case; multiple bidirectional media flows, with N=16 split evenly between 8 uplink and 8 downlink, to evaluate bandwidth fairness between the two directions; the same with on-off CBR traffic over UDP, with M=5 uplink flows ON from 0 to 60 s and OFF from 61 to 120 s; the same with off-on CBR traffic, OFF from 0 to 60 s and ON from 61 to 120 s; the same with background TCP traffic, with M=5 uplink flows from 40 s to 80 s; and a series of tests with different values of N, such as 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20, with media start times randomly distributed within 0 to 10 s and end times within 110 to 120 s.

For the downlink case each media flow is expected to get its fair share of the total bottleneck link bandwidth, and overall bandwidth usage should not be significantly lower than that experienced by the same number of concurrent downlink TCP flows, which serve as the performance benchmark, with end-to-end delay and packet loss ratio within an acceptable range for real-time multimedia. The same benchmark applies to the uplink case. With dynamic background traffic the media flows are expected to adapt in a timely fashion to the changes in available bandwidth; all downlink media flows are expected to obtain similar bandwidth as each other, and the throughput of each media flow is expected to fall when TCP background traffic arrives and rise when it leaves, for example within 10 seconds. For the varying number of flows, the results are expected to show steady and stable per-flow throughput at each value of N, with the average throughput of all media flows staying constant around the maximum rate when N is small, then gradually decreasing as N grows until it reaches the minimum allowed rate, beyond which the offered load exceeds the capacity of the Wi-Fi network.
sections.plainLanguage: The Wi-Fi cases compare a candidate algorithm against plain TCP flows doing the same thing. If sixteen media calls sharing the wireless link do noticeably worse than sixteen TCP downloads sharing it, the algorithm is not pulling its weight. The cases also add background traffic that switches on and off, to see whether the media rate reacts in time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in RFC 8868 and the relevant congestion control algorithms apply. The principles for congestion control are described in RFC 2914, and in particular any new method must implement safeguards to avoid congestion collapse of the Internet.

Given the difficulty of deterministic wireless testing, the RFC recommends and expects the tests described in it to be done via simulations. Where the test cases are carried out in a testbed instead, the evaluation should take place in a controlled lab environment, where the applications, simulators and network nodes ought to be well-behaved and should not impact the desired results. Appropriate caution is needed to avoid leaking nonresponsive traffic with unproven congestion avoidance behaviour onto the open Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a real wireless network cannot be made repeatable, these tests are meant to be run in a simulator, or in a controlled lab if a testbed run is needed. The same rule as for any congestion control work applies: nothing unproven should be let loose on the public Internet.

viz.caption: WHAT MAKES A CELLULAR LINK DIFFERENT FROM A WIRED ONE

items.title: One queue per user
items.text: The base station keeps queues per radio bearer per user, so users do not share one queue at the bottleneck as they do on a wired link.

items.title: The network sets the rate
items.text: The network part decides how much each user can transmit.

items.title: Capacity changes fast
items.text: Link capacity per user can vary within milliseconds, with distance, speed, interference and link adaptation all in play.

items.title: Handover interrupts traffic
items.text: A handover between cells can cause bursts of loss, delay and jitter, though best-effort bearers usually queue packets instead of dropping them.

items.title: Shared cost per bit
items.text: The cost per bit over the shared link varies over time and differs between users.

items.title: Two kinds of bearer
items.text: Both Quality of Service and non-QoS radio bearers can be used.

viz.caption: WHAT MAKES A WI-FI LINK DIFFERENT FROM A WIRED ONE

items.title: The radio fades
items.text: Interference, multipath fading and shadowing make the link throughput fluctuate and the environment error-prone.

items.title: Half-duplex
items.text: Bandwidth is shared between uplink and downlink traffic because the wireless medium cannot send and receive at once.

items.title: Collisions, not just queues
items.text: Traffic beyond a certain load causes contention and collisions over the air, with loss patterns unlike wired congestion.

items.title: Multi-rate links
items.text: The chosen modulation and coding scheme sets the physical-layer rate and so the application throughput.

items.title: Slow clients hold everyone back
items.text: A legacy device on a much slower link consumes a substantial share of air time and slows the rest of the network.

items.title: Handover and prioritisation
items.text: Moving between access points can cost delay and loss, and EDCA/WMM lets real-time traffic win the channel over file transfers.
